title: India's New-Generation Kabaddi Squad Begins Asian Games Title Defence
excerpt: Debutant raider Devank Dalal headlines a refreshed Indian kabaddi contingent opening its Aichi-Nagoya campaign against hosts Japan on September 21, with both the men's and women's teams defending their 2022 golds.
body:
• India's kabaddi campaign at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games begins September 21, with the men's team facing hosts Japan and the women playing Bangladesh at the Tokai Citizen Gymnasium.
  • First-time captain Sunil Kumar leads the men's squad; debutant raider Devank Dalal is the face of a new generation, while senior all-rounder Aslam Inamdar has urged teammates to "play with a free mind."
  • India enters as defending champion in both events after reclaiming the men's and women's titles at Hangzhou 2022; Iran remains the principal threat.

India's kabaddi contingent begins its title defence at the 20th Asian Games on September 21 with a squad that looks noticeably different from the one that reclaimed gold at Hangzhou four years ago. First-time captain Sunil Kumar leads the men's team onto the mat at the Tokai Citizen Gymnasium against hosts Japan, while the women's team opens against Bangladesh — the first steps in a campaign that carries the weight of a sport India considers its own.

The men's squad blends experience with youth. Aslam Inamdar, the senior all-rounder who captained Puneri Paltan to the Pro Kabaddi League Season 10 title, has taken on the role of mentor, telling younger teammates to "remain consistent, play with a free mind and understand the privilege of representing India," as quoted by IndiaSportsHub from an Olympics.com feature. The spotlight, though, is on debutant raider Devank Dalal, whose selection message was disarmingly direct: "If India has chosen me, I will have to do it."

A generational shift

Pawan Sehrawat, who captained India to gold in 2022, is in the squad but no longer wears the armband — a deliberate signal of renewal. The leadership has passed to Sunil Kumar, and the 12-man roster includes several players at their first Asian Games. It is a gamble built on confidence: kabaddi's professional ecosystem, now a decade into the Pro Kabaddi League era, has produced a deep bench, and the selectors have leaned into it.

"If India has chosen me, I will have to do it."

— Devank Dalal, India's debutant raider, on his first Asian Games selection

Aslam Inamdar's own numbers explain why his voice carries in the dressing room: 168 total points in PKL Season 10 (142 raid, 26 tackle). He has also spoken about how preparation has changed — "The S&C aspect is very important in kabaddi today. If your base is not strong, injuries are bound to happen" — reflecting a sport that has professionalised its training science since the bruising lessons of 2018.

The 2018 scar, and what followed

India dominated men's kabaddi for 24 years, winning seven consecutive Asian Games golds from 1990 to 2014. The 2018 Games in Jakarta broke that run spectacularly: Iran took both the men's and women's titles, beating India 27–24 in the women's final and pushing the men into a joint-bronze with Pakistan. It was the first time India had lost an Asian Games kabaddi match of consequence, and it forced a reckoning about complacency.

Hangzhou 2022 answered it. The men beat Iran 33–29 in the final to reclaim the crown; the women edged Chinese Taipei 26–25 in a one-point thriller to win their fourth Asian Games gold (after titles in 2010 and 2014, and the 2018 silver). India now arrives at Aichi-Nagoya defending both titles — the women chasing a second consecutive gold, the men the same.

The road to the finals

The men's group stage runs September 21–24: Japan, then Korea (Sept 22), Bangladesh (Sept 23) and Chinese Taipei (Sept 24). The women face Bangladesh (Sept 21), Iran (Sept 23) and Japan (Sept 24). The semifinals are on September 25, with the gold-medal matches on September 26.

Iran looms over both draws. The 2022 women's semifinal, where Chinese Taipei upset Iran before falling to India in the final, showed the field is deepening. For the new-look Indian squads, the test is not just skill but temperament — exactly what Inamdar's "free mind" advice targets.

What's next

Kabaddi's place at these Games doubles as a showcase. With the sport's promoters continuing to push its global footprint, another Indian double would reinforce the narrative that the professionalisation of the last decade has restored the natural order. A stumble, though — and the 2018 memories are still fresh — would reopen the questions Hangzhou was supposed to settle.
